newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's new finance chief sets reform course.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's new finance chief sets reform course.

text.p: Pakistan's new finance chief set out a sweeping reform programme on Saturday to shore up the country's crumbling economic foundations and regain the favour of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

"We are going to bust our guts in order to achieve it," Shahid Javed Burki, adviser to caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid and a World Bank vice president, told his first news conference since he took over the Finance Ministry on Friday.
Burki took a 90-day leave of absence from the World Bank after President Farooq Leghari, who sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on Tuesday, asked him to join the interim government.

The ministry's top civil servant Moeen Afzal revealed the enormity of the task ahead by saying the aim was to cut the budget deficit in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) to four percent of gross domestic product from a staggering 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
The ousted government had stated last year's budget gap at 5.0 percent of GDP when it unveiled its 1996/97 budget in June, but revised the figure to 5.8 percent of GDP last month.
Burki said Paul Chabrier, the head of the IMF's Middle East department, would arrive in Islamabad on Wednesday for talks on reactivating a stalled $600 million standby loan..
"Our expectation is that those discussions will lead to larger access to IMF funds than indicated earlier," he said, adding that the exact amounts would be decided at the talks.
He said he had begun talks before leaving Washington with IMF managing director Stanley Fisher for a cheaper, longer-term loan, or enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF).
Burki said he would lay the groundwork for a new ESAF by launching structural changes in the next few days..

He said he had set up task forces to help with fiscal reform, a public spending review, faster privatisation, trade and tariff reform, development of private sector pension funds, and "fiscal federalism", or the way the budgets of the four provinces relate to that of the federal government..
Burki said he would seek large World Bank loans to help with banking sector reforms and the formation of a "national renewal fund" intended to provide a social safety net for the poor.
In many ways Burki's programme is reminiscent of that of Pakistan's last caretaker government in 1993 under Moeen Qureshi, whose reforms led to an agreement with the IMF.

Asked if his plans might unravel when a new political government is elected on February 3, just as Qureshi's did under the Bhutto government, Burki said one important difference was that Leghari's term still has two years to run..

"We'll do this (reform programme) in a shorter period and bring about institutional changes that will be hard to monkey about with," he said, adding that the media could play a valuable role in keeping the politicians under pressure..
Burki said Pakistan's big landowners, who pay little or no income tax, would have to mend their ways. "The feudals have to be taught, told, that they have to pay their dues to society," he said.
He refused to comment on defence spending, saying he could not speak about "matters that are beyond my control".
Burki vowed to clean up the "extremely weak" banking system in which he said several institutions were insolvent, and promote reforms to strengthen Pakistan's capital markets.
The supervisory and regulatory role of the State (central) Bank of Pakistan would be strengthened and at the same time separated from the bank's role in monetary management..
Several state-owned financial institutions which had been "massively abused" and had piled up enormous debts would be scrapped, consolidated or reformed..
Their good assets would be sold and the bad ones dealt with by a new Resolution Trust Corporation, with World Bank support..
Burki said he hoped to expedite the sale of state-run United Bank Ltd within days and speed up privatisation of Habib Bank.
"Despite all the problems, I remain very optimistic of turning the economy around," Burki said. "There is a lot of political will on the part of the president and prime minister."
He said that putting good policies in place was a better way of celebrating Pakistan's 50th anniversary, which falls in 1997, than the lavish monuments now being built for the occasion. .
He said Pakistan had the potential to produce growth rates of eight to 10 percent a year. "That's our dream and I hope we will be able to achieve it," Burki declared. .
